## Concept of measure

For a general set $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ we wish to construct a function
$\mu:2^{X}\to[0,\infty]$ assigning each subset $E\subseteq X$ a number
$\mu(E)\in[0,\infty]$, some **measure** of $E$, such that:

1. for disjoint $E_{1},E_{2},\dots\subseteq X$ we have
   $\mu\left(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty E_{j}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\mu(E_{j})$
   (countable additivity);
2. for every interval $[a,b]$ we have $\mu([a,b])=b-a$; and
3. for $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$ we have
   $\mu(E+c)=\mu(E)$ (translation invariance).

The [[vitalli-non-measurability-theorem]] shows that **no such function
exists**. The closest generalisation of mass is countable additivity, which
gives rise to the **Lebesgue measure**, but not every set has a measure (for
example a Vitali set).

There are two standard ways out:

1. weaken the requirements, which leads to **outer measures**
   ([[outer-measure]]); or
2. restrict the domain to a family of **well-behaved** sets, which leads to
   **measures** and **measure spaces**.

For the second route the family of sets should be non-empty and closed under
complements and countable unions, so that it preserves the properties we want
the measure to have. Such a family is a **σ-algebra**, a special kind of
**algebra**.

## Algebras and σ-algebras

:::{.definition data-title="Algebra"}

A collection $\mathcal{A}\subseteq2^X$ is an **algebra** of subsets of $X$ if

1. $\mathcal{A}$ is non-empty;
2. it is **closed under finite unions**:
   $\{E_i\}_{i=1}^n\subseteq\mathcal{A}\implies\bigcup_{i=1}^nE_i\in\mathcal{A}$;
3. it is **closed under complements**: $E\in\mathcal{A}\implies E^c\in\mathcal{A}$.

:::

:::{.theorem}

If $\mathcal{A}$ is an algebra then

1. $\emptyset\in\mathcal{A}$ and $X\in\mathcal{A}$;
2. $\{E_i\}_{i=1}^n\subseteq\mathcal{A}\implies\bigcap_{i=1}^nE_i\in\mathcal{A}$.

:::

:::{.proof}

(1) Since $\mathcal{A}$ is non-empty there is some $E\in\mathcal{A}$, and
$E^c\in\mathcal{A}$. Then $X=E\cup E^c\in\mathcal{A}$ and
$\emptyset=X^c\in\mathcal{A}$.

(2) By [[de-morgans-laws|De Morgan's laws]],
$\bigcap_{i=1}^nE_i=\big(\bigcup_{i=1}^nE_i^c\big)^c\in\mathcal{A}$.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="σ-Algebra"}

An algebra $\mathcal{F}\subseteq2^X$ that is also **closed under countable
unions**,
$$
\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal{F}\implies\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\in\mathcal{F},
$$
is called a **σ-algebra**.

:::

:::{.theorem}

A σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ is closed under countable intersections.

:::

:::{.proof}

For $\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal{F}$, De Morgan's laws give
$$
\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty E_i=\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i^c\right)^c\in\mathcal{F},
$$
by closure under complements and countable unions.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Measurable space"}

A pair $(X,\mathcal{F})$ of a set $X$ and a σ-algebra $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets
of $X$ is a **measurable space**. Any $E\in\mathcal{F}$ is a **measurable
set**.

:::

:::{.example}

For any set $X$, both $2^X$ and the trivial σ-algebra $\{\emptyset,X\}$ are
σ-algebras. For $X=\{1,2,3\}$, the collection
$\{\emptyset,\{1\},\{2,3\},X\}$ is a σ-algebra.

:::

### Generated σ-algebras

:::{.theorem data-title="Intersection of σ-algebras"}

Given any non-empty collection $\mathcal{C}$ of σ-algebras on $X$,
$$
\bigcap\mathcal{C}:=\{E\subseteq X:E\in\mathcal{A}\text{ for all }\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{C}\}
$$
is a σ-algebra on $X$.

:::

:::{.proof}

1. $X\in\mathcal{A}$ for every $\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{C}$, so
   $X\in\bigcap\mathcal{C}$.
2. If $E\in\bigcap\mathcal{C}$ then $E\in\mathcal{A}$ and so $E^c\in\mathcal{A}$
   for every $\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{C}$, hence $E^c\in\bigcap\mathcal{C}$.
3. If $\{E_n\}\subseteq\bigcap\mathcal{C}$ then $\bigcup_nE_n\in\mathcal{A}$ for
   every $\mathcal{A}\in\mathcal{C}$, hence $\bigcup_nE_n\in\bigcap\mathcal{C}$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Generated σ-algebra"}

Given $\mathcal{E}\subseteq2^X$ there is a smallest σ-algebra containing
$\mathcal{E}$, denoted $\sigma(\mathcal{E})$ and called the σ-algebra
**generated** by $\mathcal{E}$ (see [[generated-sigma-algebra]]). Explicitly,
$$
\sigma(\mathcal{E})=\bigcap\{\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{F}\text{ is a σ-algebra on }X,~\mathcal{E}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\}.
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

The family is non-empty since $2^X$ belongs to it, so the intersection is a
σ-algebra by the previous theorem. It contains $\mathcal{E}$, and it is
contained in every σ-algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$, so it is the smallest.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Generated σ-algebra subset"}

If $\mathcal{E}\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal{A})$ then
$\sigma(\mathcal{E})\subseteq\sigma(\mathcal{A})$.

:::

:::{.proof}

$\sigma(\mathcal{A})$ is a σ-algebra containing $\mathcal{E}$, and
$\sigma(\mathcal{E})$ is contained in every such σ-algebra.

:::

The most important example is the **Borel σ-algebra** of $\mathbb{R}$,
generated by the open sets; see [[borel-measure]]. Sigma-algebras on product
spaces are treated in [[product-sigma-algebra]].

## Measures

On a measurable space we define a **measure**, a function assigning each
measurable set a size.

:::{.definition data-title="Measure"}

Given a measurable space $(X,\mathcal{F})$, a **measure**
$\mu:\mathcal{F}\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies

1. $\mu(\emptyset)=0$; and
2. (countable additivity) for disjoint $\{E_i\}_{i=1}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal{F}$,
   $\mu\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty E_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(E_i)$.

The triple $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ is a **measure space**.

:::

A measure with $\mu(X)=1$ is a probability measure and gives a
[[probability-spaces|probability space]].

:::{.example data-title="Dirac measure"}

For $(X,2^X)$ fix $x_{0}\in X$ and define
$$
\delta_{x_{0}}(A)=\begin{cases}1&x_{0}\in A,\\0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
$$
the **Dirac measure** at $x_0$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Measure properties"}

For a measure space $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ and $A,B,A_i\in\mathcal{F}$:

1. **Monotonicity:** $A\subseteq B\implies\mu(A)\leq\mu(B)$;
2. $A\subseteq B$ and $\mu(A)<\infty\implies\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$;
3. **Countable subadditivity:**
   $\mu\left(\bigcup_{i}A_{i}\right)\leq\sum_{i}\mu(A_{i})$;
4. **Continuity from below:** $A_{i}\subseteq A_{i+1}$ for all $i$ implies
   $\mu\left(\bigcup_{i}A_{i}\right)=\lim_{i\to\infty}\mu(A_{i})$;
5. **Continuity from above:** $A_{i}\supseteq A_{i+1}$ for all $i$ and
   $\mu(A_1)<\infty$ imply
   $\mu\left(\bigcap_{i}A_{i}\right)=\lim_{i\to\infty}\mu(A_{i})$.

:::

:::{.proof}

(1), (2) Write $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$, a disjoint union, so
$\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A)\geq\mu(A)$, and subtract if $\mu(A)<\infty$.

(3) Let $B_{1}=A_{1}$ and $B_{n}=A_{n}\setminus\bigcup_{i<n}A_{i}$. The $B_n$
are disjoint, $B_n\subseteq A_n$ and $\bigcup_nB_n=\bigcup_nA_n$, so
$$
\mu\left(\bigcup_{n}A_{n}\right)=\sum_{n}\mu(B_{n})\leq\sum_{n}\mu(A_{n}).
$$

(4) Let $B_{1}=A_{1}$ and $B_{i}=A_{i}\setminus A_{i-1}$ for $i\geq2$. These are
disjoint with $\bigcup_{i\le n}B_i=A_n$ and $\bigcup_iB_i=\bigcup_iA_i$, so
$$
\mu(A_{n})=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu(B_{i})\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}\sum_{i=1}^\infty\mu(B_{i})
=\mu\left(\bigcup_{i}A_{i}\right).
$$

(5) Let $B_{i}=A_{1}\setminus A_{i}$. Then $B_{i}\subseteq B_{i+1}$ and
$\bigcup_iB_i=A_{1}\setminus\bigcap_iA_i$. Since $\mu(A_1)<\infty$,
$\mu(B_i)=\mu(A_1)-\mu(A_i)$, and by (4)
$$
\mu(A_1)-\mu\left(\bigcap_iA_i\right)=\mu\left(\bigcup_iB_i\right)
=\lim_{i\to\infty}\big(\mu(A_1)-\mu(A_i)\big).
$$
Rearranging gives the result.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Finite, σ-finite, null, almost everywhere, complete"}

For a measure space $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$:

1. $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<\infty$;
2. $\mu$ is **σ-finite** if there are $\{E_{i}\}_{i=1}^\infty\subseteq\mathcal{F}$
   with $\bigcup_iE_{i}=X$ and $\mu(E_{i})<\infty$ for all $i$;
3. $E$ is a **null set** if $E\in\mathcal{F}$ and $\mu(E)=0$;
4. a property holds ($\mu$-)**almost everywhere** if the set where it fails is
   a null set;
5. $\mu$ is **complete** if every subset of a null set is measurable (and so
   has measure zero).

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Completion"}

Let $(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$ be a measure space, $\mathcal{N}=\{N\in\mathcal{F}:\mu(N)=0\}$ and
$$
\overline{\mathcal{F}}=\{E\cup F:E\in\mathcal{F},~F\subseteq N\text{ for some }N\in\mathcal{N}\}.
$$
Then $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ is a σ-algebra, the **completion** of
$\mathcal{F}$ with respect to $\mu$, and $\mu$ has a unique extension
$\overline\mu$ to a complete measure on $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$, given by
$\overline\mu(E\cup F)=\mu(E)$. The space
$(X,\overline{\mathcal{F}},\overline\mu)$ is the **completion** of
$(X,\mathcal{F},\mu)$.

:::

:::{.proof}

Since $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{N}$ are closed under countable unions, so is
$\overline{\mathcal{F}}$, and $\emptyset\in\overline{\mathcal{F}}$. For
complements, let $E\cup F\in\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ with $F\subseteq N$. Then
$$
(E\cup F)^c=E^c\cap F^c=(E^c\cap N^c)\cup\big(E^c\cap(N\setminus F)\big),
$$
where the first set is in $\mathcal{F}$ and the second is a subset of $N$.

If $E_1\cup F_1=E_2\cup F_2$ with $F_j\subseteq N_j$, then
$E_1\subseteq E_2\cup N_2$, so $\mu(E_1)\leq\mu(E_2)$, and symmetrically, so
$\overline\mu$ is well defined. Countable additivity is inherited from $\mu$,
and every subset of a $\overline\mu$-null set is in $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$.
Uniqueness follows since any complete extension must give subsets of null sets
measure zero.

:::

## Measures on the real line

One naturally asks whether there is a measure $\mu$ on the measurable space
$(\mathbb{R},\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}})$, where $\mathcal{B}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is the
Borel σ-algebra (see [[borel-measure]]), with $\mu((a,b))=b-a$ and translation
invariant. Constructing it requires [[outer-measure|outer measures]], which
are defined on all subsets, and the [[caratheodory-extension-theorem]].
